context: Current closing price of Home Depot (HD): $342.30 USD as of 2026-07-29.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from what I infer was a starting price near 342–343. For the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing level, expecting minimal drift and mean-reverting intraday dynamics to dominate, landing at 343.5. For the one-week estimate, I nudged slightly higher to 345, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the broader trend environment while acknowledging that short-term momentum can carry prices a few points in either direction. For the one-month estimate, I pushed to 348, incorporating a longer-run drift component and the historical tendency for this type of asset to trend gradually upward over multi-week periods, though the increment is deliberately modest given elevated macro uncertainty.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which is standard for any diffusion-based uncertainty framework. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 19 points, reflecting normal daily volatility and the relative predictability of the near term. At one week, the interval opens to 34 points, capturing the compounding of daily uncertainty and the possibility of a meaningful directional move driven by scheduled data releases or sentiment shifts. At one month, the interval expands to 67 points, acknowledging that over four weeks, macro surprises, earnings seasons, Federal Reserve communications, and geopolitical developments can all materially reprice the asset.

The primary sources of uncertainty are macroeconomic data surprises — particularly inflation prints, labor market reports, and central bank guidance — which can abruptly shift risk appetite and discount rate expectations. Liquidity conditions also play a role; thin trading environments can amplify moves beyond what fundamentals would imply.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include an unexpected policy shift from a major central bank, a geopolitical shock such as an escalation in an ongoing conflict, or a sudden credit event in financial markets. On the upside, a significantly better-than-expected economic data release or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could drive prices well above my upper bounds. These tail events are precisely why the stated intervals, while wide at the monthly horizon, still do not capture the full distribution of possible outcomes.
